statement: The iter-7 report of Llama-3.1-8B showing negative NSGA-II gap at rate=50 was a pop_size artifact, not a structural phenomenon. With pop_size=40 (iter-10 methodology), NSGA-II wins for Llama at rate=50 with gap=+38.6 evals (vs random reaching 95% HV at eval=117.8). The apparent random-wins pattern at rates 50-75 for Llama was specific to smaller population sizes (iter-7 unknown, likely ≤20). With pop_size=40, NSGA-II has universal advantage at both rate=50 and rate=100 for both Qwen and Llama.
regime: BLIS 6-parameter 4-objective space, pop_size=40, n_gens=4, seed=42, budget=200
mechanism: NSGA-II requires sufficient population size to maintain genetic diversity across the fitness landscape. With smaller pop_size (≤20), NSGA-II over-concentrates around early Pareto-promising regions, reducing effective coverage and potentially losing to random's uniform exploration. With pop_size=40, NSGA-II maintains enough diversity to exploit crossover yield (~15x advantage for Llama) while preserving coverage.
applicability_bounds: Applies when pop_size ≥ 40 and budget ≥ 5×pop_size. For smaller pop_size (≤20), Llama rate=50 may still show random-wins behavior. The rate breakpoint for universal NSGA-II advantage shifts when pop_size is varied.

statement: Pareto density alone is insufficient to predict NSGA-II vs random gap sign or magnitude. Additionally, crossover yield advantage (crossover_yield / pareto_density) is NOT a reliable gap-direction predictor across different model architectures and load regimes — it is uniformly high (9-17x) across all tested conditions regardless of gap sign, because it is dominated by block_size=32 concentration which is near-100% at both rate=50 and rate=100 for both models.
regime: BLIS 6-parameter 4-objective space (tp, instances, scheduler, max_batch, kv_blocks, block_size), qwen3-14b and llama-3.1-8b, rates 50 and 100
mechanism: block_size=32 dominates the Pareto front at both rate=50 (100% for both models) and rate=100 (93.5% for Qwen). When both Pareto parents have block_size=32, any crossover offspring also has block_size=32, inflating yield regardless of other parameter distributions. The crossover yield metric cannot distinguish conditions where NSGA-II advantage varies because the dominant axis (block_size) produces the same yield concentration at all load regimes.
applicability_bounds: In spaces where one binary parameter (block_size) dominates the Pareto front, crossover yield will be uniformly high. This metric would be more informative in spaces where the Pareto front varies by a continuous parameter or one without such extreme concentration.

statement: In BLIS's 6-parameter 4-objective space, block_size=32 dominates the Pareto front at rate=50 even MORE than at rate=100: 100% of Pareto configs use block_size=32 at rate=50 for both Qwen (81/81) and Llama (96/96), vs 93.5% for Qwen at rate=100. At rate=50, no block_size=16 configs are Pareto-optimal for either model. This extreme concentration drives crossover yield to ~75-79% at rate=50, higher than the ~65-67% at rate=100.
regime: BLIS, H100, rate=50, qwen3-14b and llama-3.1-8b, exhaustive 1800-config sweep
mechanism: At rate=50, the KV capacity threshold effect is slightly weaker for each individual GPU tier (lower throughput demand), but block_size=32 provides a 2x KV token capacity advantage over block_size=16 for the same kv_blocks count. At low rates, this advantage is sufficient to make block_size=16 configs Pareto-dominated across all tp/instance configurations, creating complete block_size=32 dominance. At higher rates (100), a small number of high-GPU-count configs with block_size=16 survive on the Pareto front because their raw throughput advantage outweighs the KV capacity penalty.
applicability_bounds: H100 hardware, trained-physics latency model, prefix_tokens=512, rates ≤ 50. May not hold at lower rates where more diverse workload configurations survive on the Pareto front.

statement: Crossover operator topological bias inflates baseline crossover yields above Pareto density in BLIS's configuration space. A null model (random Pareto labeling, same N) produces yields of ~21-23% regardless of condition (density ranges 4.5-6.9%, rate 50-100, either model). Null yield is 3-5x density, not ≈1x density. When interpreting crossover yield advantage, the effective signal-to-noise is crossover_yield / null_yield (~3x observed/null) rather than crossover_yield / density (9-17x observed/density). The large density-relative advantage is partly an artifact of topological bias.
regime: BLIS 6-parameter space, uniform crossover with tp×instances constraint normalization
mechanism: The crossover operator's normalize_config step (clamp num_instances to 8//tp) biases offspring toward low tp values where the instance range is largest (tp=1: 1-8 instances; tp=8: only 1 instance). Combined with uniform sampling over parameter values (not configs), the crossover output is not uniformly distributed over the config space. This topological concentration means random 'Pareto' labels produce ~21-23% null yield rather than the density-level ~5-7%. The true structural contribution of real Pareto front clustering is ~3x (observed/null), not 9-17x (observed/density).
applicability_bounds: Applies to this specific crossover operator (uniform crossover + normalize_config) in BLIS's parameter space. Other crossover operators (e.g., SBX for continuous parameters) would have different baseline biases.

statement: At rate=50 with pop_size=40, NSGA-II has a structural advantage over random search for both Qwen3-14B (gap=+55.4 evals) and Llama-3.1-8B (gap=+38.6 evals). NSGA-II advantage is universal across both models at rate=50 when using adequate population size (≥40). This extends the earlier finding (rate=100 universal advantage) to lower load regimes. At rate=100, gaps are +62.3 (Qwen) and +40.3 (Llama); at rate=50, gaps are +55.4 and +38.6 — similar magnitudes, confirming that the advantage is not rate-dependent when pop_size is held constant at 40.
regime: BLIS 6-parameter 4-objective space, H100, pop_size=40, n_gens=4, budget=200, seed=42/43
mechanism: With pop_size=40, NSGA-II maintains sufficient diversity to exploit the high crossover yield (14-17x yield advantage) in the Pareto-concentrated block_size=32 region. The multi-axis NDR structure (kv_blocks NDR ~0.75, max_batch NDR ~0.45-0.49) provides exploitable gradients that NSGA-II leverages through crossover and selection, independent of load regime.
applicability_bounds: Applies when pop_size=40 and budget=200 in the 1800-config 4-objective space. With smaller pop_size (≤20), the gap may become negative for Llama at lower rates. The pop_size threshold for universal NSGA-II advantage at rate=50 is between 20 and 40.

statement: Multi-objective search algorithm comparison (NSGA-II vs random) requires both a non-trivial Pareto frontier AND a sparse Pareto-optimal configuration set. In BLIS's corrected 6-parameter 4-objective space: Pareto density at rate=50 is 4.50% (Qwen) and 5.33% (Llama), at rate=75 is 6.06% (Qwen) and 4.83% (Llama), and at rate=100 is 6.89% (Qwen) and 5.89% (Llama). Confirmed by both iter-7 and iter-10 exhaustive sweeps. The density threshold guidance for NSGA-II advantage magnitude (>5% = moderate advantage, <5% = decisive advantage) is no longer reliable — with pop_size=40, NSGA-II wins at both 4.50% and 5.33% density at rate=50, and at both 6.89% and 5.89% at rate=100. The convergence gap is primarily determined by landscape structure (block_size=32 concentration, multi-axis NDR), not density alone.
regime: BLIS 6-parameter 4-objective space, H100, rates 50-100, Qwen and Llama
mechanism: Exhaustive sweeps at rate=50 replicate the density values from iter-7 exactly, confirming measurement stability. The density values are structural properties of the BLIS configuration space at given rate/model combinations, not algorithm-dependent.
applicability_bounds: Same as prior RP-1 plus: density values are now confirmed stable across iterations (iter-7 and iter-10 match exactly for rate=50).
